tagline: The book of beginnings: God makes a good world, humanity breaks it, and God promises to bless every nation through one family.
overview:
Genesis is the first book of the Bible and the first of the five books of the Torah, the Law of Moses, also called the Pentateuch. Its English name comes through the Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Hebrew Scriptures made from the third century BC onward) and means origin or birth. In Hebrew the book is called Bereshit, its opening word, which means in the beginning. That is exactly what it offers: the beginning of the world, of human beings, of marriage and work, of sin and death, of nations and languages, and of the people of Israel.

The book moves in two great sweeps. Chapters 1 to 11 tell the story of the whole world: God creates the heavens and the earth and makes humanity in his image; the first couple disobey and are sent out of Eden; Cain murders Abel; violence fills the earth until God sends the flood and starts again with Noah; and humanity gathers at Babel to make a name for itself and is scattered. Chapters 12 to 50 narrow to one family. God calls Abraham, promises him descendants, a land, and a blessing that will reach all the families of the earth, and then follows that promise through Isaac, through Jacob (renamed Israel) and his twelve sons, and finally through Joseph, whose brothers sell him into slavery and who rises to save Egypt and his own family from famine.

The rest of the Bible stands on this book. Its account of God as sole creator, of every person as bearing his image, of sin as a rupture between people and God, and of God's covenant promise to Abraham is assumed on almost every later page. Genesis ends with the family living in Egypt and Joseph's body in a coffin, waiting to be carried home. The promise is alive, but it is not yet kept, and the reader turns to Exodus to see what God will do.
author:
Genesis never names its author. Jewish and Christian tradition has long credited the five books of the Torah to Moses, and the New Testament speaks of these books as the law of Moses. Because Genesis describes events centuries before Moses was born, those who hold to his authorship usually say he worked from older records and oral traditions, and some suggest that the book's ten recurring headings (‘This is the account of’, Hebrew toledot) mark such earlier sources. A few details show at least some later updating, which many conservative scholars readily accept: Genesis 14:14 mentions the city of Dan, a name the town received only in the period of the judges (Judges 18:29), and Genesis 36:31 lists Edomite kings who reigned before any king reigned over Israel, a remark that assumes Israel's monarchy.

Most critical scholars since the late nineteenth century have seen the Pentateuch as a combination of several sources. The classic form of this theory, the Documentary Hypothesis associated with Julius Wellhausen, identified four documents written at different times and later woven together, three of which were found in Genesis: a strand that prefers the divine name LORD, a strand that prefers the general word God, and a priestly strand concerned with genealogies, covenants, and order. Since the 1970s that model has been heavily revised, and many scholars now speak more simply of priestly and non-priestly material, with debate over how and when they were joined. Other scholars stress the book's unified design and argue that it is better explained as the deliberate work of one author or editor using older material. Readers across these views agree that Genesis as we have it is a carefully shaped whole.
date:
The date of writing depends on the question of authorship. On the traditional view Genesis comes from the time of Moses, which places it in either the fifteenth or the thirteenth century BC, depending on how one dates the exodus (itself a contested question, with some reading 1 Kings 6:1 to place it around 1446 BC and others preferring a thirteenth-century date on archaeological grounds). Critical scholars generally date its sources between the tenth and sixth centuries BC and place the final shaping of the book in the Persian period, after the return from Babylonian exile that followed Cyrus's decree in 539/538 BC.

The events themselves are a separate question. Chapters 1 to 11 give no dates that can be tied to known history. The stories of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob have traditionally been placed in the early second millennium BC, and Joseph's rise in Egypt somewhat later, though many scholars doubt the stories can be dated at all. Since the 1970s a number of scholars have argued that the patriarchal stories reflect conditions of the first millennium BC and preserve little reliable memory of an earlier age, while others continue to argue that they fit the earlier period well. The book itself shows more interest in what God promised than in dates.
setting:
Genesis moves across the whole ancient Near East. Its first chapters look toward Mesopotamia, the land between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers, where the Sumerians and later the Babylonians built some of the world's first cities. Abraham's family comes from Ur and Harran in that region. The central chapters take place in Canaan, the land between the Jordan River and the Mediterranean, a patchwork of small city-states where the patriarchs lived as outsiders, moving their flocks between towns, digging wells, and negotiating with local rulers. The last chapters are set in Egypt, the great kingdom of the Nile, whose grain could feed its neighbors when rain failed in Canaan.

Those neighboring cultures had their own stories of beginnings. The Babylonian Enuma Elish tells of creation through a war among the gods. The Atrahasis epic tells of the gods making humans to do their labor and then sending a flood when people became too many and too noisy. The Epic of Gilgamesh includes a flood hero named Utnapishtim who builds a boat and sends out birds. The Sumerian King List names kings who reigned for thousands of years before a flood. Genesis shares some of this world's questions and imagery, but it answers them with one God, a good creation, and human beings made for dignity rather than drudgery. The first readers, whether Israel in the wilderness after Egypt or Israel in the long aftermath of exile in Babylon, needed to hear exactly that difference.
purpose: Genesis tells Israel who its God is and why it exists. It shows that the LORD who called Abraham is no local deity but the maker of heaven and earth, that the world's brokenness comes from human rebellion rather than from the nature of things, and that God answered that rebellion not by abandoning the world but by choosing one family through whom he would bless all the others. It explains why Israel had a claim to the land of Canaan, why it traced its tribes to twelve brothers, and how it came to be in Egypt, which sets the stage for the exodus. For any later reader, it answers the oldest questions about where we came from, what we are for, what went wrong, and whether God has given up on us.
story: Genesis is where the story begins, so nothing comes before it except God himself. Everything after it depends on it. Exodus opens with Jacob's descendants multiplying in Egypt, becoming slaves, and being rescued, which is the first great fulfillment of the promise that Abraham's offspring would become a nation. The covenant at Sinai, the entry into the land under Joshua, and the kingdom of David each carry forward the promises of offspring, land, and blessing made in Genesis 12 to 22. The exile seems to undo them, and the prophets look beyond it to a new start. The New Testament presents Jesus as the one in whom those promises are finally kept, and the Bible's last chapters return to images from Genesis 2, a river of life and the tree of life, in a new creation where the curse is gone.
christ:
The New Testament reads Genesis as the opening of the story that Christ completes. After the first sin God tells the serpent that the woman's seed will crush its head (Genesis 3:15). Christian readers since at least the second century, Irenaeus among them, have heard in this the first announcement of the gospel, while many modern interpreters read it first as a promise of humanity's long struggle with evil; Paul echoes it when he writes, “The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet” (Romans 16:20). Paul calls Adam “a pattern of the One to come” (Romans 5:14), the first head of humanity whose failure Christ reverses.

The promise to Abraham is the book's backbone, and Paul says that in it God “foretold the gospel to Abraham” (Galatians 3:8). He reads the promised seed as fulfilled in Christ (Galatians 3:16), and he holds up Abraham, who believed God and was counted righteous (Genesis 15:6), as the model of faith for Jew and Gentile alike (Romans 4). Hebrews finds in Melchizedek, the priest-king of Salem, a pattern for Christ's priesthood (Hebrews 7), and in Abraham's offering of Isaac a faith that expected God to raise the dead (Hebrews 11:17-19). Jacob's blessing of Judah in Genesis 49:10 is of a different kind: a formal oracle about the future, promising that the scepter will not depart from Judah until the one comes to whom it belongs. Its Hebrew is difficult, but Jewish interpreters read it of the Messiah before and alongside the church, in the Dead Sea Scrolls commentary on Genesis (4Q252) and in the Aramaic paraphrase Targum Onqelos. Other links are patterns rather than predictions: Joseph, rejected by his brothers and then raised up to save them, has long been seen as a picture of the rejected and exalted Christ.
reading: Genesis is narrative, with poetry at key moments (2:23, 3:14-19, 49) and genealogies that serve as its skeleton rather than filler. Watch for the recurring heading ‘This is the account of’ (toledot), which opens each of the book's ten sections after the prologue and names the starting point whose story follows, and for the patterns the book repeats: the younger son preferred over the older, barren wives who conceive only by God's intervention, a patriarch passing off his wife as his sister (chapters 12, 20, and 26), and blessings and curses spoken over children. The narrator rarely stops to pass moral judgment, so describing an act is not the same as approving it; the consequences usually do the judging. Two misreadings are common. One treats the patriarchs as moral heroes to copy, when the book presents them as flawed people carried by a faithful God. The other reduces chapters 1 to 11 to a question of science versus myth. Readers differ on how literally to take those chapters, but the book's own concern is who God is, who we are, and how God keeps his word.

structure.title: Prologue: the seven days of creation
structure.summary: Before the first heading, God creates the heavens and the earth by his word, makes humanity male and female in his image, calls everything very good, and rests on the seventh day, which he blesses.

structure.title: The account of the heavens and the earth
structure.summary: The first heading (2:4) tells what came of the created world: the man and woman in Eden, the command and the fall, exile east of Eden, Cain's murder of Abel, the spread of Cain's line, and the birth of Seth, when people begin to call on the name of the LORD.

structure.title: The book of the generations of Adam
structure.summary: Opening with ‘the book of the generations of Adam’ (5:1), a ten-generation genealogy runs from Adam to Noah with its refrain ‘and then he died’, broken by Enoch, who walked with God. It closes with the sons of God and human violence, the LORD's grief, and Noah finding favor.

structure.title: The account of Noah
structure.summary: Noah, righteous and blameless, builds the ark; the flood undoes creation and God remembers Noah. Afterward God makes a covenant with Noah and every living creature, sets the rainbow as its sign, and grounds the value of human life in the image of God, and Noah's drunkenness exposes Ham.

structure.title: The account of Noah's sons
structure.summary: The Table of Nations (10:1) lists seventy peoples descended from Shem, Ham, and Japheth, spread across the known world. The story of Babel (11:1-9) then tells how humanity, united in language, tried to make a name for itself and was scattered.

structure.title: The account of Shem
structure.summary: A second ten-generation genealogy (11:10) narrows from Shem to Terah and his three sons, Abram, Nahor, and Haran, carrying the line of blessing through the scattered nations toward Abraham.

structure.title: The account of Terah: Abraham
structure.summary: Under Terah's heading (11:27) comes the story of his son Abram: the call and the promise of land, offspring, and blessing for all nations; covenant, circumcision, and a new name; the long wait for Isaac; the binding of Isaac; and Abraham's burial in the one piece of land he owned.

structure.title: The account of Ishmael
structure.summary: A short record (25:12) of Ishmael's twelve sons shows God keeping his promise to make Hagar's son a great nation, before the story returns to the chosen line.

structure.title: The account of Isaac: Jacob
structure.summary: Under Isaac's heading (25:19) comes the story of his twin sons. Jacob takes Esau's birthright and blessing, flees to Harran, builds a family of twelve sons amid rivalry, wrestles with God and is renamed Israel, returns to the land, and buries his father.

structure.title: The account of Esau
structure.summary: Esau's line becomes the nation of Edom. The heading appears twice (36:1 and 36:9, the second locating Esau in the hill country of Seir), and the chapter lists Edom's chiefs and its kings who reigned before any king in Israel, while Jacob settles in Canaan (37:1).

structure.title: The account of Jacob: Joseph and his brothers
structure.summary: The last heading (37:2) introduces the story of Jacob's sons. Joseph is sold into Egypt, rises to rule under Pharaoh, and saves the family from famine; Judah offers himself for Benjamin; the brothers are reconciled; Jacob blesses his sons; and Joseph dies trusting God to bring Israel home.

themes.title: Blessing and curse
themes.body: God's first word to humanity is a blessing (1:28), and sin brings curse on the serpent and the ground (3:14-17), on Cain (4:11), and on Canaan (9:25). The call of Abraham answers that spread of curse with a fivefold repetition of blessing (12:1-3). The rest of the book traces who receives the blessing, how it is passed on, and how it reaches outsiders such as Laban and Potiphar and finally Pharaoh and all Egypt through Joseph.

themes.title: The promised offspring
themes.body: The word seed, or offspring, runs from 3:15 through the promises to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Yet the promise keeps meeting obstacles: barren wives, murdered sons, famine, a father told to sacrifice his heir, brothers who try to kill one of their own. Genesis shows that the line of promise survives because God preserves it, not because the family is strong or good.

themes.title: The land
themes.body: God promises Abraham the land of Canaan, but Abraham lives in it as a foreigner and owns only a cave for a grave (chapter 23). Jacob spends twenty years away from it and his sons end the book in Egypt. The land is promised, walked through, and longed for, and Joseph's final request to have his bones carried there leaves the promise pointing forward into Exodus and Joshua.

themes.title: God's choice of the unlikely
themes.body: Again and again God passes over the expected heir: Abel and then Seth rather than Cain, Isaac rather than Ishmael, Jacob rather than Esau, Joseph and Judah rather than Reuben, Ephraim rather than Manasseh. The pattern overturns the ancient assumption that the firstborn inherits by right and shows that God's purposes rest on his free choice and grace.

themes.title: Providence through human failure
themes.body: The people of Genesis lie, scheme, play favorites, and betray one another, and God works through all of it without excusing any of it. The theme comes to its clearest statement at the end, when Joseph tells his brothers that what they intended for evil God intended for good (50:20). Genesis teaches that God's plan is not derailed by human sin, which is both a comfort and a warning.

keyChapters.why: God creates the world by his word and makes humanity, male and female, in his image. The foundation of the Bible's teaching on God, creation, and human dignity.
The first disobedience, its consequences, and the first hint of hope in the promise about the woman's seed. Everything that goes wrong in the Bible's story traces back here.
After the flood God makes a covenant with Noah and every living creature, promising never again to destroy the earth by flood, and grounds the value of human life in the image of God.
God calls Abram and promises him a great nation, a great name, and blessing for all the families of the earth. The hinge on which the whole Bible turns from the world's story to Israel's.
Abram believes the LORD and it is credited to him as righteousness, and God binds himself by covenant in a strange night ceremony. Paul builds his teaching on faith on this chapter.
God tests Abraham by commanding him to offer Isaac, then provides a ram in his place. One of the most searching and most discussed stories in Scripture.
Jacob wrestles through the night with a mysterious man, is renamed Israel, and walks away limping and blessed. The nation takes its name from this encounter.
Joseph forgives his brothers and names God's providence over their evil, and he dies trusting God to bring Israel back to the promised land.

text:
Genesis is carefully preserved, and English Bibles differ over it far less than over some other books, but the witnesses do diverge in ways a reader will notice.

The standard Hebrew text is the Masoretic Text, transmitted by Jewish scribes (the Masoretes) who added vowel signs and accents in the early Middle Ages. Its oldest complete manuscript is the Leningrad Codex, copied in 1008 or 1009 and the basis of modern printed Hebrew Bibles; the older Aleppo Codex (tenth century) lost nearly all of the Torah after the anti-Jewish riots in Aleppo in 1947. The Dead Sea Scrolls include about twenty fragmentary copies of Genesis from Qumran and nearby sites, from the second century BC to the first century AD, and they agree closely with the Masoretic Text. Three other witnesses matter most. The Samaritan Pentateuch, preserved by the Samaritan community, differs from the Masoretic Text in thousands of small spellings and in some real readings. The Septuagint, the Greek translation made in Alexandria from the third century BC, was the Bible of most New Testament writers. The Aramaic Targums (Onqelos, Neofiti, and Pseudo-Jonathan), the Syriac Peshitta, and Jerome's Latin Vulgate (translated from the Hebrew around 390 to 405) show how the text was read.

The largest differences are in the numbers. In the genealogies of chapters 5 and 11 the three main witnesses give different ages at which the fathers had their sons: the Septuagint often adds a hundred years, which lengthens the span from creation to the flood and from the flood to Abraham by several centuries, and it adds a generation, Cainan, between Arphaxad and Shelah (11:12-13), which Luke 3:36 follows. That is one reason chronologies built from Genesis disagree. Other differences surface in translations. At 4:8 the Hebrew says Cain spoke to Abel without reporting what he said; the Samaritan Pentateuch, Septuagint, Syriac, and Vulgate supply ‘Let us go out to the field’, which many modern versions adopt. At 47:31 the same Hebrew consonants can be read as bed (mittah, the Masoretic reading) or staff (matteh, the Septuagint), and Hebrews 11:21 follows the Septuagint's staff. At 2:2 the Septuagint and Samaritan read that God finished his work on the sixth day rather than the seventh.

Chapter and verse numbers came later (chapter numbers in the Middle Ages, verse numbers in the sixteenth century, though the Hebrew verse divisions themselves are much older), and at one place the Hebrew and English numbering differ: English 31:55 is Hebrew 32:1, so the verses of chapter 32 are one higher in Hebrew Bibles (English 32:1-32 is Hebrew 32:2-33). The Hebrew tradition divides the book differently, into paragraphs marked by open and closed spaces and into twelve weekly synagogue readings.
reception:
Genesis has been read more intensively than almost any book in the world. Jewish writers of the Second Temple period retold it: the Book of Jubilees (second century BC) recast it by a calendar of jubilees and made the patriarchs keep the law; the Genesis Apocryphon from Qumran retold the stories of Noah and Abraham in Aramaic; Philo of Alexandria read it as allegory of the soul's ascent; and Josephus retold it in the first book of his Jewish Antiquities (about AD 93 to 94). The rabbis gathered their interpretations in Genesis Rabbah, edited in the land of Israel in the early fifth century, and the Targums paraphrased it in Aramaic for the synagogue. The great medieval commentators wrote on it at length: Rashi (eleventh century), Abraham ibn Ezra, David Kimhi (Radak), and Nahmanides (Ramban, thirteenth century), whose principle that the deeds of the fathers are a sign for the children read the patriarchs' travels as a pattern for Israel's history. In the synagogue Genesis is read in twelve weekly portions each autumn and winter, beginning just after Simchat Torah, and the binding of Isaac (Genesis 22) is read on the second day of Rosh Hashanah.

Christian reading began in the New Testament itself, with Paul's arguments from Adam (Romans 5), from Abraham's faith (Romans 4, Galatians 3), and from Sarah and Hagar read allegorically (Galatians 4:24), and with Hebrews 11's roll of the faithful from Abel to Joseph. The church fathers produced a library on Genesis: Origen's homilies, Basil's nine homilies on the six days (378), John Chrysostom's sixty-seven homilies preached at Antioch, Ambrose's treatises on Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph, Ephrem the Syrian's commentary, and Augustine's several works on the opening chapters, capped by The Literal Meaning of Genesis (401 to 415) and books 11 to 16 of the City of God. Medieval readers studied it through the Glossa Ordinaria and Thomas Aquinas's treatise on the six days. Luther's lectures on Genesis (1535 to 1545) were the last great work of his life, and Calvin's commentary appeared in 1554.

Modern criticism began largely with Genesis. Spinoza's Theological-Political Treatise (1670) questioned Mosaic authorship, Jean Astruc (1753) noticed that the divine names might mark different sources, and Julius Wellhausen's Prolegomena (1883) gave the Documentary Hypothesis its classic form. Hermann Gunkel's commentary (1901) read the stories as folk sagas; Gerhard von Rad and Claus Westermann wrote the major twentieth-century German commentaries; and Umberto Cassuto, Nahum Sarna, and Robert Alter led Jewish and literary readings of its unity. Genesis has been at the center of every debate about science and Scripture since Darwin.

Its life in culture is enormous. Kierkegaard's Fear and Trembling (1843) meditates on Genesis 22; Erich Auerbach's Mimesis (1946) opens by setting the binding of Isaac beside Homer; Thomas Mann retold the Jacob and Joseph stories in the four novels of Joseph and His Brothers (1933 to 1943). Michelangelo's Sistine ceiling (1508 to 1512) paints its first chapters, Rembrandt painted the sacrifice of Isaac (1635) and Jacob blessing Joseph's sons (1656), Haydn set the creation to music (1798), and Benjamin Britten staged the flood for children in Noye's Fludde (1958).

furtherReading.author: Derek Kidner
furtherReading.title: Genesis: An Introduction and Commentary
furtherReading.note: A short, clear evangelical commentary that handles the hard questions briefly and wisely; still one of the best first companions to the whole book.

furtherReading.author: Tremper Longman III
furtherReading.title: How to Read Genesis
furtherReading.note: An accessible guide to reading Genesis as literature, history, and theology, including its ancient Near Eastern background and its place in the Bible's story.

furtherReading.author: Robert Alter
furtherReading.title: Genesis: Translation and Commentary
furtherReading.note: A literary scholar's translation that keeps the Hebrew's repetitions and wordplay, with brief notes on how the stories are told.

furtherReading.author: Walter Brueggemann
furtherReading.title: Genesis
furtherReading.series: Interpretation: A Bible Commentary for Teaching and Preaching
furtherReading.note: A mainline Protestant commentary written for preachers, strong on the book's theology and its address to faith today.

furtherReading.author: Nahum M. Sarna
furtherReading.title: Genesis
furtherReading.note: A Jewish commentary on the Hebrew text that joins ancient Near Eastern background with classical rabbinic interpretation; excellent on the stories' world.

furtherReading.author: Bruce K. Waltke with Cathi J. Fredricks
furtherReading.title: Genesis: A Commentary
furtherReading.note: An evangelical commentary that reads each episode as literature and draws out its theology, with attention to the book's structure.

furtherReading.author: John H. Walton
furtherReading.title: Genesis
furtherReading.note: Strong on the ancient Near Eastern setting and on moving from the ancient meaning to preaching and teaching today.

furtherReading.author: Andrew Louth, editor
furtherReading.title: Genesis 1-11
furtherReading.note: Selections from the church fathers, Greek, Latin, and Syriac, arranged verse by verse on the opening chapters.

furtherReading.author: R. R. Reno
furtherReading.title: Genesis
furtherReading.series: Brazos Theological Commentary on the Bible
furtherReading.note: A Catholic theologian's reading of Genesis within the church's doctrinal tradition, in conversation with the fathers.

furtherReading.author: Gordon J. Wenham
furtherReading.title: Genesis 1-15
furtherReading.note: A detailed evangelical commentary on the Hebrew text, strong on literary structure and ancient parallels; continued in Genesis 16-50 (1994).

furtherReading.author: Victor P. Hamilton
furtherReading.title: The Book of Genesis: Chapters 1-17
furtherReading.series: New International Commentary on the Old Testament
furtherReading.note: A thorough evangelical commentary on the Hebrew, with notes on how the New Testament uses each section; a second volume covers chapters 18 to 50.

furtherReading.author: Claus Westermann
furtherReading.title: Genesis 1-11: A Commentary
furtherReading.note: The massive German critical commentary in John Scullion's translation, unmatched in its survey of ancient parallels and earlier scholarship.

furtherReading.author: Umberto Cassuto
furtherReading.title: A Commentary on the Book of Genesis, Part I: From Adam to Noah
furtherReading.note: A Jewish scholar's close reading of chapters 1 to 6, arguing for the unity of the text and alert to its numerical and verbal patterns.

furtherReading.author: Gerhard von Rad
furtherReading.title: Genesis: A Commentary
furtherReading.note: A classic of twentieth-century German Protestant scholarship, reading the book through its sources and its theology of promise.

furtherReading.author: Ronald Hendel
furtherReading.title: The Book of Genesis: A Biography
furtherReading.note: A short history of how Genesis has been read, from ancient Israel through Jewish and Christian interpreters to modern science and literature.

parts.body:
Genesis is the first book of the Bible. Its name comes from Greek and means ‘origin’ or ‘birth’. In Hebrew the book is called Bereshit, its first word, which means ‘in the beginning’. It has 50 chapters.

The book tells of beginnings: the world, human beings, marriage and work, sin and death, the nations and their languages, and the people of Israel. It begins with God speaking light into darkness. It ends with a coffin in Egypt.

Genesis moves in two halves. Chapters 1 to 11 tell the story of the whole world. God makes a good world and makes human beings in his image. They turn from him, and the damage spreads: a murder, a flood, a proud tower. Chapters 12 to 50 narrow to one family. God calls Abraham and makes him a promise: a people, a land, and a blessing for “all the families of the earth” (12:3). The rest of the book follows that promise through Isaac, Jacob and Jacob's twelve sons, and through Joseph, sold as a slave by his brothers, who rises to save them.

Almost every later page of the Bible stands on this book. Its claims are large and simple: one God made everything; every person bears his image; sin is a break between people and God, not just a mistake; and God answered that break with a promise, not with giving up. The book ends with the promise alive but not yet kept. The reader turns to Exodus to see what God will do.

parts.h: The first book of the Torah
parts.body:
Genesis is the first of five books that belong together: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers and Deuteronomy. Jews call them the Torah. The word means ‘teaching’ or ‘instruction’, though it is often put into English as ‘law’. Christians often call the same five books the Pentateuch, a Greek word for a work in five volumes. Jesus and the apostles call them ‘Moses’ or ‘the Law’.

Genesis is the doorway into the Torah. The other four books tell how God rescued Israel from slavery in Egypt, made a covenant with them at Mount Sinai, gave them his law, and led them to the edge of the land he had promised. Genesis tells why any of that happened. It answers the questions a freed people would ask. Who is this God who brought us out? Why did he choose us? Why this land? How did we end up in Egypt?

The links are deliberate. In Genesis 1 God blesses the first humans: “Be fruitful and multiply, and fill the earth” (1:28). Exodus opens with the same words come true in Israel: “the Israelites were fruitful and increased rapidly; they multiplied and became exceedingly numerous, so that the land was filled with them” (Exodus 1:7). The blessing given to all humanity is now growing in one family, as God promised Abraham.

The ending of Genesis also points forward. Joseph, dying in Egypt, says, “God will surely visit you and bring you up from this land to the land He promised on oath to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob” (50:24). He makes his brothers promise to carry his bones home. Exodus begins where that promise is still waiting.

So Genesis is not a separate book of old stories. It is the first part of one long account, and much of what it says only becomes clear as that account goes on.

parts.h: Who wrote it, and how we know
parts.body:
Genesis never names its author. No verse says who wrote it. What we have instead is a long tradition, some clues in the text itself, and more than two centuries of debate among scholars.

The tradition. Jewish and Christian readers have long credited the five books of the Torah to Moses. The New Testament speaks of “the Book of Moses” (Mark 12:26), and Jesus says of Moses, “he wrote about Me” (John 5:46). Since Genesis tells of events long before Moses was born, those who hold that he wrote it usually say he worked from older records and memories handed down in Israel.

What the text shows. A few details seem to come from a time after Moses. Genesis 14:14 says Abraham chased his enemies “as far as Dan”, but Judges 18:29 says the town got that name much later; before, it was called Laish. Genesis 36:31 lists the kings of Edom who reigned “before any king reigned over the Israelites”, which sounds like a writer who knew Israel had kings. Many who hold to Moses as the main author accept that later hands updated such details.

The documentary hypothesis. In 1753 a French doctor, Jean Astruc, noticed that Genesis 1 calls God only ‘God’, while other passages use his personal name, the LORD. He suggested Moses had used separate sources. Later scholars built this into a theory of four written sources, given letters J, E, D and P, woven together over centuries. Its classic form came from the German scholar Julius Wellhausen, whose book of 1878 appeared in a second edition in 1883 as the Prolegomena to the History of Israel. On that view Genesis was woven from three of the sources.

Later models. From the 1970s, books by John Van Seters (1975), Hans Heinrich Schmid and Rolf Rendtorff (1977) questioned the old theory, especially its early date for the J source. Scholars have not agreed on what should replace it. Many now speak more simply of ‘priestly’ and ‘non-priestly’ material. Others think the books grew by stages of additions. A revised form of the four-source view still has defenders, especially in North America and Israel.

Conservative replies. The Jewish scholar Umberto Cassuto, in lectures published in Hebrew in 1941 and in English in 1961, argued that the change in God's names is chosen for meaning, not a sign of different sources: ‘God’ for the Creator of all, ‘the LORD’ for the God who comes near to his people. Others argue that the stories fit an earlier world better than the theory allows. In 1936 P. J. Wiseman suggested that the headings ‘these are the generations of’ were the closing lines of older tablets that Moses gathered; most scholars have not been persuaded.

What to make of it. Readers on every side agree that Genesis as we have it is a carefully shaped whole. Christians who confess the Bible as God's word hold more than one of these views. These notes do not settle the question, and the book's authority does not hang on knowing the writer's name.

When Genesis was written depends on who wrote it, so the answers follow the views on authorship. Two settings are proposed most often, and each helps a reader hear the book.

Israel leaving Egypt. On the traditional view, Genesis comes from the time of Moses, when Israel had just left slavery in Egypt and was on the way to Canaan. That puts it in the 1400s or the 1200s BC, depending on how the exodus is dated, which is itself debated. Imagine those first hearers: freed slaves who had grown up among Egypt's many gods, about to enter a land full of other gods. Genesis told them who their God was: not one god among many, but the maker of everything, including the sun and the Nile. It told them why the land was theirs to receive, and that their story began with a promise made to their ancestors long before Egypt.

Israel in exile. Many critical scholars date the book's sources between about the tenth and the sixth centuries BC, and its final shaping to the years after the exile. In 597 and again in 586 BC the Babylonians took the people of Judah away to Babylon. In 539 BC Cyrus of Persia took Babylon, and some of the exiles returned. Read in that setting, Genesis speaks straight into Babylon's shadow. Genesis 1 answers Babylon's own creation story (see ‘Genesis and its neighbors’ below). The Hebrew name Babel in Genesis 11 is the same word the Bible uses for Babylon. And Abraham's family begins in Mesopotamia, the land of the exile, and is called out of it toward the land of promise.

Either way, Genesis speaks to people who are not yet home. Its heroes live in tents in a land they do not own. Abraham buys only one piece of it, a field with a cave for a grave (chapter 23). Jacob says his years have been “few and hard” (47:9). The book ends outside the land, with a coffin waiting to be carried back. For a people waiting on God, in the wilderness or in exile, that was the point. The promise was older than their trouble, and God had kept faith with their ancestors through worse.

These notes do not choose between the settings. A reader can hear the book in both, and many readers do.

Genesis has a frame of its own, built into the text. Again and again a new section begins with the same words: “This is the account of” (2:4). The Hebrew, elleh toledot, means literally ‘these are the generations of’. The word toledot comes from the verb ‘to give birth’. It names what came out of a starting point.

The heading opens ten sections: 2:4, 5:1, 6:9, 10:1, 11:10, 11:27, 25:12, 25:19, 36:1 and 37:2 (with a repeat at 36:9). Each one names a starting point and then tells what came of it. So ‘the account of Terah’ is mostly about Terah's son Abraham, and ‘the account of Jacob’ is mostly about Jacob's son Joseph. The first heading is unusual: “the account of the heavens and the earth” (2:4). It tells what came of the world God made.

Before the first heading stands a prologue, the seven days of creation (1:1 to 2:3). It is the frame around the whole book: one God, a good world, human beings in his image, and a day of rest.

The book then falls into two halves.

Chapters 1 to 11: the world. Creation, the garden and the fall, Cain and Abel, the long family line from Adam to Noah, the flood, the nations spread out over the earth, and the tower of Babel. The story is wide and fast. Whole centuries pass in a list of names.

Chapters 12 to 50: one family. The pace slows almost to a walk. Three long stories carry this half: Abraham (11:27 to 25:11), Jacob (25:19 to 35:29) and Joseph (37 to 50). Isaac's story sits between his father's and his son's.

Two short sections deserve notice: the accounts of Ishmael (25:12-18) and Esau (36). These are the sons who were not chosen to carry the promise. Genesis still gives each a heading and a family line. God kept his word to them too, and the book does not forget them.

The pattern is narrowing and widening. The story narrows from all humanity to Shem's line, to Abraham, to Jacob's sons. But it narrows for the sake of the wide world: through this family “all the families of the earth will be blessed” (12:3). At the end, Joseph's food feeds Egypt and the lands around it.

The outline band at the top of this page draws these parts. Tap a part to read its summary.

parts.h: What kind of writing it is
parts.body:
Genesis is mostly narrative: stories told in order, with people, places and speech. Three other kinds of writing are woven in, and each needs its own way of reading.

Family lines. Lists of names (chapters 5, 10, 11, 36) can look like filler. In Genesis they are the skeleton. They show time passing, the promise moving down the generations, and death reigning over every life: in chapter 5 almost every entry ends “and then he died”. When a line breaks the pattern, as Enoch's does (5:24), the reader should notice.

Poetry. At key moments speech turns into poetry: the man's cry when he sees the woman (2:23), God's words after the first sin (3:14-19), and Jacob's blessings on his sons (chapter 49). Poetry is compact and full of images. It is read slowly.

The seven days. Genesis 1 is written in prose, but it is built like a hymn. Each day repeats the same phrases: God said, ‘Let there be’, it was so, God saw that it was good, evening and morning. Days one to three make spaces (light and dark, sky and sea, dry land). Days four to six fill them (lights, birds and fish, animals and people). The seventh day breaks the pattern: no work, and no closing evening and morning.

Ancient, not modern, history-writing. Genesis tells about the past as ancient writers did. It chooses what to tell and leaves much out. It shapes its stories to teach who God is and who we are. It rarely stops to judge what its people do; often it simply reports and lets the results do the judging. A reader should not assume that because Genesis describes something, it approves of it.

How literal are chapters 1 to 11? Here faithful Christians differ, and some differ sharply. Some read the days of Genesis 1 as ordinary days and hold that the earth is young. Others read them as long ages, or as a literary frame, or as God's workdays, or as the setting up of the world as God's temple. Others hold that God created through the long process biology describes. Christians also differ on whether Adam was one historical man and how he relates to the first human beings. The site's Honest Answer ‘How should a Christian read Genesis 1?’ sets out six readings, each in its defenders' best form, with its hard question. Christians differ, and these notes do not settle it.

What every one of those readings confesses together is not small: God made everything that is, from nothing, by his word; the world is good; and every human being bears his image. Those claims are the chapter's main business on any reading.

Israel did not live alone. The great peoples around it told their own stories about how the world began and about a great flood. Several of those stories have been dug up and read. Setting them beside Genesis shows both how much Genesis shares with its world and how sharply it differs.

Enuma Elish. This is Babylon's creation story, named from its first words, ‘when on high’. The best copies come from the library of the Assyrian king Ashurbanipal at Nineveh, from the 600s BC, though the poem itself is older. George Smith first published it in 1876. In it the god Marduk goes to war against Tiamat, the goddess of the salt sea. He kills her, splits her body, and makes the sky from one half and the earth from the other. Then humans are made from the blood of a slain rebel god, Kingu, so that they can do the gods' work.

Atrahasis. An older Babylonian poem, known from a fairly complete copy of about 1650 BC. The gods are tired of digging canals and farming. So a god is killed, and the mother goddess mixes his flesh and blood with clay to make human beings to carry that work. People multiply, and their noise keeps the chief god, Enlil, awake. He sends plague, then drought, then a flood. The god Enki warns the wise man Atrahasis, who builds a boat and survives.

Gilgamesh. In the eleventh tablet of this famous poem, a man named Utnapishtim tells how the gods sent a flood and how he survived it in a great boat. When the boat comes to rest he sends out a dove, which comes back, then a swallow, which comes back, then a raven, which does not. The best known copy, in the British Museum, is from the 600s BC. On 3 December 1872 George Smith read his translation of it to a learned society in London.

What is alike. Humans made from earth or clay. A flood that wipes out life. One man warned, a boat built, birds sent out (Noah sends a raven and then a dove, 8:6-12), and a sacrifice after the waters go down.

What is different. In Genesis there is one God, not many. There is no battle: God speaks, and the sea obeys. The sun and moon are not even named; they are ‘lights’ hung in the sky to mark time. Human beings are not slaves made to feed the gods. They are made in God's image, and God feeds them (1:29). The flood does not come because people are noisy. It comes because “the earth was corrupt in the sight of God, and full of violence” (6:11). And afterwards God binds himself by a covenant to every living creature (9:8-17).

How to explain the likeness? Some scholars think Genesis borrows these stories and answers them. Others think the stories share a common memory or a common stock of images. Many hold that Genesis speaks the language of its world on purpose, to say something new in it. These notes do not choose. The differences are the heart of the matter. The site's guide ‘Was Genesis 1 Answering Babylon, Not Modern Science?’ tells this story at more length.

Creation and blessing. God's first word to human beings is a blessing (1:28). Then sin brings curse: on the serpent, on the ground, on Cain. In chapter 12 God answers the spreading curse with a promise of blessing, repeated five times in three verses (12:1-3). The rest of the book traces who receives the blessing and how it spreads to outsiders, until Joseph's wisdom feeds all Egypt.

The image of God. Human beings, “male and female” (1:27), are made in God's image. In the ancient world a king set up his image to show his rule. Genesis gives that dignity to every person, not only kings. The image is not lost after the first sin: Genesis 5:1 and 9:6 still speak of it, and 9:6 makes it the reason murder is so grave.

Sin and its spread. Chapter 3 tells of the first disobedience. After it, sin grows: a brother murders a brother (chapter 4), violence fills the earth (chapter 6), and the builders of Babel set out to “make a name for ourselves” (11:4). Each time, God judges, and each time, he also shows mercy: clothing, a protecting mark, an ark, and finally a call to Abraham.

Promise and covenant. God promises Abraham offspring, land and blessing. He binds himself by covenant (chapters 15 and 17) and swears an oath (chapter 22). The rest of the book tests the promise again and again: wives who cannot have children, famine, a son on an altar, brothers who want to kill one of their own. The promise survives because God keeps it, not because the family is strong or good.

Chosen for the sake of the nations. God chooses one family, but not against the others. Abraham is blessed so that “all the families of the earth will be blessed through you” (12:3). Being chosen is a task, not a trophy.

The younger chosen over the elder. In the ancient world the firstborn son normally inherited. Genesis keeps turning that upside down: Abel and then Seth rather than Cain; Isaac rather than Ishmael; Jacob rather than Esau (“the older will serve the younger”, 25:23); Joseph and Judah rather than Reuben; Ephraim rather than Manasseh. God's choice rests on his grace, not on birth order.

Deception and its harvest. Genesis does not hide its heroes' lies. Jacob tricks his father, whose eyesight had failed, with the skins of young goats (27:16). Years later his uncle Laban tricks him on his wedding night, and his own sons deceive him by dipping Joseph's robe in a young goat's blood (37:31). The book lets the harvest of deceit speak for itself.

Providence in Joseph. Providence means God's care and rule over what happens. In Joseph's story God is rarely seen acting openly. Yet at the end Joseph says to his brothers, “what you intended against me for evil, God intended for good” (50:20). This does not excuse the brothers. It says that their evil was not the last word.

parts.h: The covenants with Noah and Abraham
parts.body:
A covenant (Hebrew berit) is a binding promise that creates a lasting bond. The word appears 27 times in Genesis. Two covenants carry the book.

With Noah, and every living creature. After the flood God says, “Behold, I now establish My covenant with you and your descendants after you, and with every living creature that was with you” (9:9-10). He promises that never again will a flood destroy the earth. The sign is the rainbow (9:13). This covenant asks nothing in return. It is God binding himself, and it reaches every animal and every human being, not only one people. In the same chapter God says that human life is precious “for in His own image God has made mankind” (9:6).

With Abraham. God's call in chapter 12 holds three promises: a great nation, a land, and blessing for all families of the earth. Chapter 15 turns the promise into a covenant in a strange night scene. Abraham cuts animals in half and lays the halves opposite each other. After dark “a smoking firepot and a flaming torch appeared and passed between the halves of the carcasses” (15:17). Jeremiah later explains the custom: those who break a covenant are treated “like the calf they cut in two in order to pass between its pieces” (Jeremiah 34:18). To walk between the pieces was to say, ‘May this happen to me if I break my word.’ In Genesis 15 only the fire, the sign of God, passes through. God takes the weight of the promise on himself.

The same chapter holds one of the most quoted lines in the Bible: “Abram believed the LORD, and it was credited to him as righteousness” (15:6). Abraham is counted right with God because he trusted God's promise.

In chapter 17 God gives the covenant a sign, circumcision, and new names: Abram becomes Abraham, “for I have made you a father of many nations” (17:5), and Sarai becomes Sarah. In chapter 22, after Abraham's test, God confirms the promise with an oath.

How it fits later. Israel's covenant at Mount Sinai in Exodus follows the shape of ancient treaties between a great king and a people he had rescued. The site's guide ‘What Is a Biblical Covenant?’ explains that shape. Genesis lays the ground for it: before God gives any law, he makes promises, and he keeps them.

Abraham, Isaac and Jacob are called the patriarchs, a word meaning ‘founding fathers’. Their world is far from ours, and what is known about it helps a reader picture the stories. It also has limits, and honest readers name them.

Ur and Haran. Abraham's family sets out “from Ur of the Chaldeans” and settles for a time in Haran (11:31). Ur was a great city in southern Mesopotamia, near the Euphrates. A British and American team led by Leonard Woolley dug there from 1922 to 1934. Its patron god was the moon god, called Nanna, or Sin in Akkadian. The moon god was also the chief god of Haran, far to the north. Joshua 24:2 says Abraham's father Terah “worshiped other gods”. The family that God calls is a family of the moon god's cities.

‘Of the Chaldeans’. The Chaldeans were a people who settled in southern Mesopotamia later, by about the 800s BC. Some scholars take the phrase as a sign that the story was written down, or updated, in later times, using the name readers knew. Others reply that no earlier name for the area is known, so the label proves little.

Herders among towns. The patriarchs live in tents, move their flocks between towns, dig wells and make agreements with local rulers. They are outsiders. Abraham buys his wife's grave and weighs out “four hundred shekels of silver” for it (23:16); silver was weighed, not counted in coins.

Customs. When Sarah cannot have a child, she gives her slave Hagar to Abraham, “perhaps I can build a family by her” (16:2). The Laws of Hammurabi, from about 1754 BC, have rules for a similar case (laws 144 to 147), though there it concerns a wife who was a priestess and not allowed to bear children. Those laws also say that such a slave mother who claims equality with her mistress may not be sold. The parallel is real but not exact.

The Nuzi tablets: a caution. From the 1930s to the early 1970s many scholars explained the patriarchs' customs by tablets found at Nuzi, in northern Iraq. Rachel's theft of her father's household gods (31:19), for example, was said to be a claim on his inheritance. Since the 1970s, studies by Thomas Thompson (1974) and John Van Seters (1975) and others have questioned much of this. The Nuzi tablets come from the 1400s and 1300s BC. Only about a dozen of some four thousand are quoted again and again. And the household-gods reading no longer holds even for the Nuzi texts themselves. Scholars now use the Nuzi parallels with caution.

Camels. Camels appear in the stories of Abraham, Jacob and Joseph. A 2013 study by Tel Aviv University found that domesticated camels in the Aravah valley, south of the Dead Sea, appear mostly from the last part of the 900s BC. Some take the camels in Genesis as written in the terms of a later age. Others reply that camels were rare but known earlier, and the debate goes on.

Genesis gives many ages and spans of years, but it never ties its story to a king or event that can be dated from outside the Bible. So any date for Abraham is worked out, not read off the page.

The traditional placing. Adding up the Bible's own numbers, such as the 430 years in Egypt (Exodus 12:40) and the 480 years from the exodus to Solomon's temple (1 Kings 6:1), has led many readers to place Abraham early in the second millennium BC, roughly four thousand years ago. In the twentieth century the archaeologist W. F. Albright placed the patriarchs between about 2100 and 1800 BC and linked Abraham to wandering herders of that age. Kenneth Kitchen, an Egyptologist, defended a second-millennium setting for the stories, for example in a well-known article of 1995.

The later placing. In the 1970s Thomas Thompson (1974) and John Van Seters (1975) argued that there is no convincing evidence for a second-millennium setting. Van Seters held that the names, the social world and the message of the stories fit a much later age, the Iron Age of Israel's kings. Some go further and doubt that the stories preserve any memory of real people. Others hold that the stories are old memories told in later words.

What archaeology can and cannot show. Families of herders who live in tents and move with their flocks leave very little behind. Archaeology can describe the world the stories might fit, in more than one century. It cannot confirm or rule out one family moving through Canaan with its flocks. Arguments from what has not been found, such as the camel bones, are real, but they can change with the next dig.

What can be dated. The earliest mention of Israel outside the Bible is on a stone set up by the Egyptian king Merneptah in about 1208 BC. It names Israel as a people. That is centuries after the traditional date for Abraham, and it tells us nothing about him directly.

So the question is open. Christians who trust Genesis hold more than one view of when the patriarchs lived and how the book's numbers work. These notes do not settle it. Genesis itself cares more about what God promised than about dates.

parts.h: How the New Testament reads Genesis
parts.body:
The writers of the New Testament read Genesis as the start of the story that Jesus completes. Here are the main places where they take it up.

“In the beginning.” John opens his Gospel with the same words as Genesis: “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1:1). He says that this Word, who became a man in Jesus, is the one through whom God made the world: “Through Him all things were made” (John 1:3). The God who speaks in Genesis 1 speaks through his Word.

Adam and Christ. Paul sets Adam beside Jesus in Romans 5. “Sin entered the world through one man, and death through sin” (Romans 5:12). Adam is “a pattern of the One to come” (Romans 5:14): one man whose act affects all who belong to him. “Through the disobedience of the one man the many were made sinners, so also through the obedience of the one man the many will be made righteous” (Romans 5:19). He says it again more briefly: “For as in Adam all die, so in Christ all will be made alive” (1 Corinthians 15:22).

Abraham's faith. Paul builds his teaching on faith on Genesis 15:6: “Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness” (Romans 4:3). He points out that this came before Abraham was circumcised (Romans 4:10), so Abraham is the father of all who believe, Jews and Gentiles alike. In Galatians 3 Paul says the Scripture “foretold the gospel to Abraham” when it promised that all nations would be blessed through him (Galatians 3:8), and he reads the promised ‘seed’ as Christ (Galatians 3:16).

Melchizedek. In Genesis 14 a priest-king of Salem blesses Abraham and receives a tenth from him, then vanishes from the story. Psalm 110:4 speaks of a coming king who is “a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek”. Hebrews 7 joins the two. It reads even Genesis's silence about Melchizedek's family as a picture: “Without father or mother or genealogy, without beginning of days or end of life, like the Son of God, he remains a priest for all time” (Hebrews 7:3).

Faith that looks ahead. Hebrews 11 walks through Genesis, from Abel to Joseph. Abraham went out “without knowing where he was going” (Hebrews 11:8), and when he offered Isaac he “reasoned that God could raise the dead” (Hebrews 11:19).

Marriage and the new creation. Jesus answers a question about divorce from Genesis 1 and 2 (Matthew 19:4-5). The last pages of the Bible return to the garden: “a tree of life” beside a river, and “No longer will there be any curse” (Revelation 22:2-3).

These readings are the New Testament's own. Genesis was first heard in its own world, and it is worth hearing there before it is heard again in the light of Christ.

parts.h: How Jews and Christians have read it
parts.body:
Genesis is Israel's Scripture first. It was read and loved in Israel for centuries before there was a church, and it is still read in synagogues week by week. In traditional Jewish practice the story of the binding of Isaac (chapter 22) is read on the second day of Rosh Hashanah, the Jewish New Year. Christians who read Genesis are reading a book they share with the Jewish people, and they do well to read it with respect for how Jews have read it.

Christian readers have argued over Genesis from the start, and not only in modern times. In the third century Origen asked how there could be a first, second and third day, with evening and morning, before the sun was made on the fourth. In the fourth century Basil of Caesarea preached nine sermons on the six days and took them in their plain sense. Early in the fifth century Augustine wrote The Literal Meaning of Genesis and concluded that the days were not days measured by the sun. The church has held more than one faithful reading from the beginning. The Honest Answer on Genesis 1 tells this story with their own words.

A vile misuse: ‘the curse of Ham’. Genesis 9:20-27 tells how Noah got drunk and lay uncovered in his tent, and how his son Ham saw him and told his brothers. When Noah woke, he said, “Cursed be Canaan! A servant of servants shall he be to his brothers” (9:25). Notice who is cursed. It is Canaan, Ham's son, not Ham. Nothing in the passage says anything about skin, colour or race.

Yet for centuries this passage was twisted. From about the fifteenth century the curse was moved from Canaan to Ham and tied to Black Africans. Many writers and preachers used this so-called ‘curse of Ham’ to claim that God had made Africans to be slaves. In America it was preached from pulpits to defend slavery and, later, segregation. This teaching is false and evil. These notes name it and reject it. The text curses Canaan, not Ham, and it says nothing about Africa or about race. In the same chapter God says that every human being is made “in His own image” (9:6). Some medieval Jewish commentators, among them Ibn Ezra and Nahmanides, already pointed out that the curse touched only the one person named and had nothing to do with dark skin.

The church's misuse of this chapter caused real and lasting harm, so it must be named wherever Genesis is taught. Read for what it says, the passage is a story of shame: a son who exposed his father, two who covered him, and family sin passing down the generations.

hard.line: ‘In the beginning’: the start of everything, and how to read the six days. The readings Christians hold, and why these notes take no side on the age of the earth or on evolution.
‘Let Us make man in Our image’. Who is ‘Us’? The main readings, and what it means that male and female alike bear God's image.
A second account of creation, with a new name for God and a different order. How the two accounts relate, and the main views.
The woman's seed and the serpent's head: the ‘first gospel’ reading, the plainer reading, and how they fit together.
Where did Cain's wife come from? What the text says (5:4), and what it does not stop to explain.
The ‘sons of God’ and the daughters of men: angels, the line of Seth, or rulers. Three old readings, stated fairly.
‘The LORD regretted that He had made man’. Can God regret, when 1 Samuel 15:29 says he does not change his mind?
Noah's curse falls on Canaan, not Ham. The so-called ‘curse of Ham’, once used to defend the slavery of Africans, is a vile misuse of this text, named and rejected.
The tower of Babel: what the builders wanted, why God scattered them, and how Acts 2 answers the story.
Sodom, Lot's offer of his daughters and their later acts: what the text reports without approving, and how later Scripture names Sodom's sins.
God tells Abraham to offer his son. One of the hardest stories in the Bible, faced honestly.
The violence done to Dinah and her brothers' brutal revenge. A story Genesis tells without excusing anyone.
Judah and Tamar: a widow wronged, a trick, and a father-in-law who says, “She is more righteous than I”.

words.line: Hebrew ‘in the beginning’, the first word of the Bible and the Hebrew name of the book. John's Gospel opens with the same words (John 1:1).
The usual Hebrew word for God. It is plural in form, but used of Israel's God it takes a singular verb: in 1:1 ‘God created’, not ‘they created’.
God's personal name, four Hebrew letters probably said ‘Yahweh’. English Bibles print it LORD in small capitals. It first appears in 2:4.
To create. In the Bible only God does this. It appears 53 times in the Old Testament, 11 of them in Genesis, first in 1:1.
Image. Kings set up images of themselves to show their rule. Genesis says every human being, male and female, is made in God's image (1:27).
Adam means ‘human being’ or ‘man’; adamah means ‘ground’. The man is formed from the ground (2:7), and to the ground he returns (3:19).
‘A helper suitable for him’ (2:18). Of the word's 21 uses in the Old Testament, most describe God himself helping his people (Psalm 121:1-2). It does not mean a lesser rank.
‘Generations’ or ‘account’, from the verb ‘to give birth’. ‘This is the account of’ opens each main section of Genesis; the word appears 13 times in the book.
Covenant: a binding promise that makes a lasting bond. It appears 27 times in Genesis, first with Noah (6:18) and then with Abraham.
Seed or offspring. Like ‘seed’ in English it can mean one child or a whole line. It runs from 3:15 through every promise to Abraham's family.
Blessing. God's first word to people is a blessing (1:28), and his call to Abraham repeats it again and again (12:1-3).
The new name given to Jacob ‘because you have struggled with God and with men, and you have prevailed’ (32:28). It became the name of his whole people.
‘Formless and void’ (1:2): a world empty and without order, not yet fit to live in. The days of creation shape it and then fill it.

timeline.what: God creates the heavens and the earth (1:1). Genesis gives no date, and Christians differ on how to read the six days.
From Adam to Noah, ten generations (chapter 5), then the flood and God's covenant with every living creature (6 to 9).
The nations spread out, Babel is scattered, and ten generations run from Shem to Abraham (10:1 to 11:26).
Abraham leaves Ur and Haran for Canaan (11:31 to 12:9). Many readers place him early in the second millennium BC; others think the stories cannot be dated.
Isaac, the son of promise, and Jacob, who is renamed Israel and has twelve sons (21 to 35).
Joseph is sold into Egypt, rises to rule under Pharaoh, and brings his family there in a famine (37 to 50).
The Laws of Hammurabi are carved in Babylon, with rules for a slave woman who bears children for a wife, as Hagar does for Sarah.
The oldest fairly complete copy of the Babylonian poem Atrahasis, with its story of humans made from clay and a great flood.
The Nuzi tablets are written in northern Mesopotamia. Scholars once leaned on them to explain the patriarchs' customs; they now use them with caution.
On the traditional view, Moses writes the Torah in the time of the exodus. The date depends on when the exodus happened, which is debated.
An Egyptian stone of King Merneptah names Israel as a people: the earliest mention of Israel outside the Bible.
Domesticated camels appear in the Aravah valley, according to a 2013 study, part of the debate over the camels in Genesis.
The library of the Assyrian king Ashurbanipal at Nineveh holds copies of Enuma Elish and of the Gilgamesh flood tablet.
Babylon takes the people of Judah into exile. In 539 BC Cyrus of Persia takes Babylon, and some exiles return.
Many critical scholars date the final shaping of Genesis and the Torah to the Persian period, after the exile.
The Torah is translated into Greek for Greek-speaking Jews in Egypt, the first part of the Septuagint, the Greek Old Testament.
The French doctor Jean Astruc notices that parts of Genesis call God ‘God’ and others ‘the LORD’, and suggests Moses used sources.
George Smith reads his translation of the Gilgamesh flood tablet in London (1872) and publishes Enuma Elish (1876).
Julius Wellhausen's Prolegomena gives the four-source theory of the Torah its classic form.

places.name: Ur
places.line: Abraham's family sets out from ‘Ur of the Chaldeans’ (11:28-31). Ur is usually placed at Tell el-Muqayyar in southern Mesopotamia, where it is drawn here; some have proposed a northern Ur near Haran instead.

places.name: Haran
places.line: Terah's family settles here on the way to Canaan, and Abraham leaves from here at seventy-five (11:31 to 12:4). Jacob later flees here to his uncle Laban and works for him twenty years (chapters 29 to 31).

places.name: Paddan-aram
places.line: The country around Haran. Rebekah's family lives here, and Jacob is sent here to find a wife (25:20; 28:2). Drawn roughly, near Haran.

places.name: Canaan
places.line: The land God promises to Abraham and his children (12:5-7; 17:8). The second map below shows it close up.

places.name: Goshen
places.line: Abraham goes down to Egypt in a famine (12:10). Later Jacob's family settles in Goshen, in Egypt, when Joseph brings them there (45:10; 47:27). Goshen is usually placed in the eastern Nile delta; it is drawn here roughly.

places.name: Dothan
places.line: In the hills north of Shechem. Joseph finds his brothers here with the flocks, and they throw him into a pit and sell him (37:17-28).

places.name: Shechem
places.line: Abraham's first stop in Canaan, where God promises the land and Abraham builds an altar (12:6-7). Jacob later camps here, and Dinah is attacked here (chapter 34).

places.name: Bethel
places.line: Abraham pitches his tent near here. Jacob dreams of a stairway to heaven and names the place Bethel, ‘house of God’ (28:10-22).

places.name: Moriah
places.line: ‘The land of Moriah’, where Abraham is sent to offer Isaac (22:2). Where exactly is uncertain. 2 Chronicles 3:1 names Mount Moriah as the site of Solomon's temple in Jerusalem, so it is drawn there, roughly.

places.name: Bethlehem
places.line: Rachel dies giving birth to Benjamin and is buried ‘on the way to Ephrath (that is, Bethlehem)’ (35:19).

places.name: Hebron (Mamre)
places.line: Abraham settles by the oaks of Mamre at Hebron (13:18), where three visitors come to him (chapter 18). He buys a cave here to bury Sarah (chapter 23). Mamre is usually placed just north of the town.

places.name: Beersheba
places.line: Abraham digs a well and swears an oath with Abimelech here (21:22-33). Isaac lives here, and Jacob sets out from here for Haran (28:10).

places.name: The plain of the Jordan
places.line: Lot chooses this well-watered plain and settles near Sodom (13:10-12). Where Sodom stood is not known: some place it south of the Dead Sea; others north of it.

places.name: Sodom
places.line: The city Lot settles near (13:12), destroyed in chapter 19. Where it stood is not known. It is drawn at the south end of the Dead Sea, one of the places proposed, roughly.

places.name: Peniel
places.line: By the ford of the Jabbok, a river that runs down into the Jordan from the east, Jacob wrestles until dawn. He calls the place Peniel, ‘face of God’ (32:22-31). The exact spot is uncertain.

places.name: Gilead
places.line: The hill country east of the Jordan. Laban catches up with Jacob here, and they set up a heap of stones as a witness between them (31:21-55).

teaching.mapNote: Two maps. The first follows the family from Ur and Haran to Canaan and down to Egypt. The second shows Canaan close up, where most of the story happens.
